title: Synchronization, Kinematic Waves and Spike-Phase-Separation in Feedback Ising Neural Networks on Heterogeneous Graphs
authors: Anna Poggialini, Irem Topal, Fabrizio Lombardi, Daniele De Martino
abstract: Structural heterogeneity constrains collective dynamics in complex systems. However, its analytical tractability out of equilibrium remains limited. In this work, we study a class of kinetic Ising neural networks driven out of equilibrium by a homeostatic feedback loop between the neuronal excitability and the population firing rate. Using a Curie-Weiss heterogeneous mean-field approximation validated by Monte Carlo simulations, we provide an analytical characterization of how a macroscopic synchronized limit cycle emerges via an Andronov-Hopf bifurcation on heterogeneous networks. We derive closed-form phase boundaries and show that the onset of oscillations is explicitly controlled by network heterogeneity through the degree moment ratio. Degree heterogeneity decouples the spiking rate per neuron m from the spiking rate per synapse u, generating physical phenomena absent in homogeneous systems. These include (i) kinematic waves of sequential, degree-ordered activations propagating from the network periphery to the hubs, and (ii) a low-temperature phase-separated state emerging via a pitchfork bifurcation. We prove that for highly heterogeneous topologies, this phase-separated fixed point stabilizes and dynamically destroys the synchronized limit cycle. These results provide a mathematical framework for understanding how heterogeneity regulates macroscopic oscillations and out-of-equilibrium transitions in neural networks
summary: This paper analyzes the collective dynamics of Ising neural networks on heterogeneous graphs, focusing on how structural disorder modifies out-of-equilibrium behavior. Using mean-field theory, the authors predict that heterogeneity causes distinct physical phenomena, including propagating kinematic waves and phase separation. These findings provide a mathematical toolset for understanding how network topology regulates macroscopic oscillations in complex systems.
main_problem: The study investigates how structural heterogeneity constrains collective dynamics and state transitions in complex, out-of-equilibrium systems like neural networks.
main_result: Degree heterogeneity decouples neuron firing rate from synapse firing rate, leading to novel phenomena such as kinematic waves and a phase-separated low-temperature state that can destroy synchronized oscillations.
method: The authors use the Curie-Weiss heterogeneous mean-field approximation combined with linear stability analysis and bifurcation theory to characterize these transitions analytically.
model_or_system: The system is a kinetic Ising neural network driven out of equilibrium by a homeostatic feedback loop. The dynamics are governed by spin flip rates derived from an effective Hamiltonian, analyzed via degree-resolved magnetizations.
key_observables: Global magnetization ($m$), per-edge average neighbor magnetization ($u$), and the bifurcation threshold ($ eta_c(c)$) determining the onset of oscillations.
important_parameters: Degree heterogeneity quantified by the degree moment ratio $\alpha = \langle k^2 angle / \langle k angle$, and feedback strength $c$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Curie-Weiss heterogeneous mean-field approximation, which simplifies the complex dynamics into tractable equations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate phase diagrams in the $(c,  eta)$ plane showing regions corresponding to different dynamical phases (limit cycle vs. fixed point) and show time series confirming oscillatory behavior and wave propagation signatures.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the system dynamics via a master equation to deriving mean-field equations for degree-specific magnetizations. It then uses linear stability analysis to find bifurcation points, characterizes novel collective behaviors (waves/phase separation), and concludes by mapping out the full phase diagram in parameter space.
why_interesting: The mathematical framework developed for analyzing non-equilibrium transitions using mean-field theory and bifurcation analysis is highly relevant to understanding critical phenomena in open quantum systems or complex many-body dynamics where external feedback plays a role.
